U2A's output also goes to a circuit known as the Squelch. The squelch, as you may recall, has the job of quieting the receiver whenever a signal is not present. Let's see how it works.

T1 and X1 are the primary resonant filters that allow only the 455 kHz IF signal and its sidebands located at 450 kHz and 460 kHz to pass into the amplifier U4 on pin 4.
The outputs of the mixer are sent to pins 4 & 5 of U4. All frequencies created during the heterodyning process are present on those pins.

There will be the two original frequencies as well as the sum and difference of those frequencies. The 455 kHz frequency, with it's upper and lower sidebands, needs to be amplified. All other frequencies will be filtered out in the IF amplifier section.
The desired, resultant output is a modulated 455 kHz frequency that contains the intelligence from the original RF signal. However, as a product of heterodyning, other frequencies are created.

The mixer portion of U3 then heterodynes the original RF and the LO frequency.e the received signal is only measurable in microvolts and is not of sufficient amplitude to be used, as is, by the receiver.

When sound waves are applied to the microphone they are converted to audio frequency and then fed to the audio amplifier, U2. The amplifier brings the audio frequency up from several millivolts to a usable level of several hundred millivolts.
The condenser microphone used by the Nida CB Trainer operates under the same basic idea, but utilizes electrical capacitance to produce the audio frequency as opposed to a mechanical device.
